question: After Juju accepts a reprovision request for a lost machine and moves it back to pending, what message does the machine's status carry, and what extra data does that status record about the old cloud instance?
ground_truth: The machine (and its cloud instance) status is set to pending with the message "reprovisioning requested"; the status data holds one key, "old-instance-id", containing the ID of the instance that was detached.
key_facts: status message is "reprovisioning requested"
machine status and instance status are both set to pending
status data contains the key "old-instance-id" with the detached instance ID

question: A container machine is hosted on a parent machine, and both have been flagged as needing a reboot. What action is the container told to take, and what happens if only the parent is flagged versus only the container?
ground_truth: The container is told to shut down (not reboot) whenever its parent is flagged for reboot, regardless of its own flag, since the parent's reboot takes the container down anyway. If only the container is flagged it reboots; if neither is flagged it does nothing.
key_facts: parent flagged -> container action is shutdown, even if the container is also flagged
only the container flagged (parent not flagged or no parent) -> reboot
neither flagged -> do nothing
the parent's flag is checked first; only a parent and no grandparent is supported

evidence.quote: return nil // early exit, no need to check current machine reboot, it will shutdown anyway

question: I removed a machine from the model and the removal keeps being retried with the error "cannot delete machine ..., it hosts has 1 unit(s)". What causes this, and what makes the machine deletion go through?
ground_truth: A non-forced machine deletion counts the units on the machine's network node whose life is not dead; if any remain, it fails with this error (marked as machine-has-units and as an incomplete removal job, so it is retried). It succeeds once all units on the machine are dead/removed, or if the removal is forced, which skips the dependents check.
key_facts: the error is raised when units hosted on the machine are not yet dead (unit life != dead)
the job is flagged as incomplete so it is retried later
forcing the removal skips the dependents check
dependents also include child containers and storage (filesystems/volumes)

evidence.quote: cannot delete machine %q, it hosts has %d unit(s)

question: How many times can a single machine be reprovisioned before Juju stops trying and marks it as permanently failed?
ground_truth: The documentation does not say: no maximum number of reprovisions, retry counter or permanent-failure state is defined; the only guard is that a reprovision request cannot be made while one already exists for the machine.
key_facts: no reprovision count or limit is defined
greps: grep -rniE 'reprovision.*(retries|attempt)|reprovision.*count|reprovision.*(cap|threshold|quota)' -> no results (only unrelated Capture matches)

question: What port does the Juju controller's embedded SSH server listen on by default, and what restrictions apply if I set a different port in the controller configuration?
ground_truth: The default SSH server port is 17022 (config key ssh-server-port). A configured value must be a positive integer and must not equal the controller's api-port.
key_facts: Default ssh-server-port is 17022
The value must be positive (non-positive is rejected as not valid)
The value must not match api-port

question: When a unit of the controller application is removed from the controller model, what happens to the matching controller node record, and what is deleted versus kept?
ground_truth: Only for the controller application in the controller model, the unit's number is used as the controller ID. The node is first marked dying (life 1), then its API/client/agent/peer addresses, reported agent version, password, nonce and upgrade info rows are deleted, and finally it is marked dead (life 2) with its dqlite node ID and bind address set to NULL. The controller_node row itself is retained as a tombstone so delayed controller workers cannot recreate it.
key_facts: Applies only to the controller application in the controller model, using the unit number as controller ID
Node goes to dying, dependent rows (addresses, agent version, password, nonce, upgrade info) are deleted
Node is then marked dead with dqlite_node_id and dqlite_bind_address cleared
The controller_node row is kept as a tombstone

question: I ran `juju destroy-controller` on my controller without any extra flags and it refused with "The controller has live models". Why does it do this and how do I proceed?
ground_truth: The command checks the hosted models and, if any is still alive and --destroy-all-models was not given, fails with 'cannot destroy controller "<name>"' / 'The controller has live models', listing them. Re-run the command with the --destroy-all-models option.
key_facts: Error text: cannot destroy controller "<name>" ... The controller has live models
Cause: hosted models are still alive and --destroy-all-models was not specified
Fix: run destroy-controller again with --destroy-all-models

evidence.quote: The controller has live models. If you want
run this command again with the --destroy-all-models

question: Does Juju keep a history of controller configuration changes, and can I roll the controller configuration back to an earlier revision?
ground_truth: The documentation does not say; no controller configuration history or rollback is defined. Controller config is stored as a current key/value table, updates upsert or delete keys in place.
key_facts: No history or revision of controller config is defined
No rollback operation exists

question: Which access levels can be granted to a user on a cloud?
ground_truth: Only two levels are valid on a cloud: add-model and admin.
key_facts: add-model is a valid cloud access level
admin is a valid cloud access level
No other level (read, write, consume, login, superuser) is valid on a cloud

question: If I revoke the superuser level from a user on the controller, what access do they end up with? And what happens to their access if I then revoke login as well?
ground_truth: Revoking superuser on a controller downgrades the user to login. Revoking login then leaves no access, and the user's permission record on the controller is deleted.
key_facts: Revoking superuser on a controller gives login access
Revoking login on a controller results in no access
When the resulting access is none, the permission row is deleted rather than updated

question: I ran a grant giving a user read access on a model, and it failed with a message saying the user already has the access "or greater". What causes this and what should I do?
ground_truth: The error reads: user "<name>" already has "<level>" access or greater. It occurs when the user's current access level on the target is equal to or greater than the level being granted (e.g. granting read to a user who already has read, write or admin). Nothing needs changing; to give a different level, grant a strictly higher one (or revoke first to lower it).
key_facts: Message format: user "<name>" already has "<level>" access or greater
Cause: the user's existing level on that target is equal to or greater than the requested level
Grant only succeeds if the requested level is strictly higher than the current one (otherwise the existing permission is left unchanged)

question: Can I grant a user access to a model or offer for a limited time, so that the permission expires automatically after a set duration?
ground_truth: The documentation does not say; no expiry, TTL or time-limited permission concept is defined for permissions.
key_facts: No expiry/TTL field exists on permissions
The documentation does not define time-limited grants

grep -riE 'temporary access|temporary grant|time-limited|timelimited|grant.{0,20}(ttl|duration|until|valid_until|expires)' over whole code -> only firewall/API port test helpers (unrelated)

grep -riE '(expir|ttl|lifetime|validity|notafter)' in core/permission, domain/access/state/permission.go, cmd/juju/model/grantrevoke*.go -> no matches

question: When I import SSH keys into a model from an external service instead of pasting them, which prefixes can I put in front of the account name, and which service does each one stand for?
ground_truth: Two prefixes are understood: gh: (GitHub, e.g. gh:tlm) and lp: (Launchpad, e.g. lp:~wallyworld). Any other scheme is rejected as an unknown import source.
key_facts: gh: imports keys from GitHub
lp: imports keys from Launchpad

At service/facade level an unknown scheme yields UnknownImportSource ('cannot import from key source %q for user %q, unknown source'); but the juju import-ssh-key CLI Init rejects other prefixes first with 'prefix in Key ID ... not supported, only lp: and gh: are allowed'.

question: A model is migrated into this controller from an older 3.x controller where the SSH keys were still stored in the model's configuration. What happens to those keys during import, which user ends up owning them, and are all of them kept?
ground_truth: The keys are read from the model config 'authorized-keys' value and split into individual keys. Any key whose text contains the comment juju-system-key (the old controller's own key) is discarded with a warning so the source controller cannot ssh in after migration. The remaining keys are added to the model under the admin user.
key_facts: keys come from the 'authorized-keys' entry in the migrated model config
keys containing the comment 'juju-system-key' are dropped, with a warning logged, to stop the source controller keeping access
all remaining keys are added to the admin user for the imported model

question: I added several SSH keys to my user, and 'juju ssh' to a model through the controller fails with 'public key ... used to authenticate is not associated with model ...'. What does this error mean and how do I fix it?
ground_truth: The key presented during authentication is one of the user's controller-wide registered keys, but keys are added per model, and the key being used has not been added to the target model (after the user's SSH access to the model was already confirmed). Add that key to the model, or connect with a different key that is associated with the model.
key_facts: error text: public key %q used to authenticate is not associated with model %q, add the key to the model or specify a different key
authentication is controller scoped but keys are added per model, so the model membership is checked once the model is known
the check happens after the user's SSH access to the model has passed
fix: add the key to the model or present another key that is associated with it

evidence.quote: is not associated with model %q, add the key to the model or specify a different key
The key used during authentication is controller scoped, but keys are
inModel, err := a.access.HasPublicKeyInModel(ctx, ctx.User(), userKey.PublicKey, destination)

question: What is the maximum number of SSH keys that can be added to a model, or to a single user on a model, before further additions are refused?
ground_truth: The documentation does not say: no limit on the number of SSH keys per model or per user is defined.
key_facts: no maximum or quota on the number of keys is defined
